say: Welcome. This is Soap Chemistry, Materials and Safety for Production, module 1 of our soap making course.
Before a big batch, you need good materials, a safe space, and exact grams. Let's look at each one.

shots.label: PKO, palm oil, coconut oil, shea
say: Look at these oils. Soap is made by reacting oils with caustic soda, and the reaction gives you soap and glycerin.
Palm kernel oil, which we call PKO, and coconut oil give strong cleansing. Palm oil and shea butter give a hard bar with creamy lather.
Smell before you buy. A sour smell means the oil is going rancid. And never use frying oil.

shots.label: Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide)
say: Now look closely. This white, flaky material is sodium hydroxide, which the market calls caustic soda.
Good flakes are dry and loose, like these, from a sealed bag or tub.
Wet, sticky or clumped flakes have taken in water from the air and lost strength. Don't buy that bag.

shots.label: Caustic soda pearls
say: Caustic soda also comes as these small white beads, which sellers call pearls.
Flakes and pearls weigh and dissolve in much the same way, so buy whichever your supplier keeps fresh and sealed.
Avoid big solid lumps, and avoid liquid caustic soda in kegs, because you cannot know its strength.

shots.label: Sealed, labelled tub
shots.banner: Never keep caustic soda in drink bottles
say: Watch how it is stored: lid closed tight, raised off the floor, away from water, acids and aluminium, out of reach of children.
People in Nigeria have been seriously injured by swallowing caustic soda kept in drink bottles. Mark every container: caustic soda, poison.

shots.label: Clean, soft water
say: Here is the water. Use clean, soft water: filtered rain water, or boiled and cooled borehole water.
Hard or iron-rich water can cause spots and scum in the bar.

shots.label: Goggles, long gloves, apron
say: Before you open the caustic soda bag, put these on.
Sealed splash goggles, not ordinary glasses. Long gloves covering your wrists. Long sleeves, an apron and closed shoes, and a dust mask while you weigh flakes.
Mix your lye outdoors, or under a roof with open sides, never in a closed kitchen.
Keep children, pets and visitors out while you work.

shots.label: Caustic soda INTO water
shots.banner: Never pour water onto caustic soda
say: Now watch carefully. Cold water is weighed into a stainless steel or strong plastic container. The caustic soda is weighed in a separate dry one.
We add the caustic soda to the water, slowly, a little at a time, stirring with a stainless spoon. Never the other way round.
See the heat rising? It can go above 80 degrees Celsius, so step back from the fumes for a minute.
Never use aluminium, tin or zinc pots or spoons.
Now cover it loosely, label it, and let it cool where nobody can knock it over.
If caustic soda splashes on skin, rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes. Don't use vinegar. Water is the correct treatment.
For eyes, rinse for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelids open, then go to hospital.

shots.label: Scale reading in 1 g steps
say: Every batch starts with exact grams, never cups or tins.
Zero the scale with the empty container on it, then write each weight on your batch sheet and tick it.

card.title: 1 kg laundry test batch
card.note: Blessing's batch sheet, from the course worked example

say: Here is how Blessing in Aba works out a 1 kg test batch of 70% PKO and 30% palm oil.
She multiplies each oil's grams by its SAP value from the table, which gives 165.8 g of caustic soda.
For a laundry bar she takes off 2% superfat: 162.5 g. Her caustic soda is 98% pure, so she divides by 0.98 and weighs 166 g of flakes.
Water is 162.5 times 67, divided by 33: 330 g. Copy this card.
That superfat is spare oil left in the bar. We use 2% for laundry bars, so clothes are not left oily, and 5% for bath bars.

Well done. Now go through the lessons below, and do the practice task: draw your safety layout and build your first batch sheet.
